lessons.title: How communication works
lessons.html:
The communication process

Communication is passing a message from a sender to a receiver so that it is understood. In an abattoir, poor communication can cause unsafe meat, injuries and conflict. A supervisor communicates all day: with workers, other supervisors, the meat inspector, maintenance, the office and management.

Steps in communication

  1. The sender has a message.
  2. The sender chooses the channel: speaking, a written note, a notice, a radio, an e-mail or a phone call.
  3. The receiver gets the message and interprets it.
  4. The receiver gives feedback, showing whether the message was understood.

Barriers to communication

  • Noise: machines, saws and compressors make it hard to hear.
  • Language: teams speak many languages, such as isiZulu, isiXhosa, Sesotho, Setswana, Afrikaans and English.
  • Jargon: technical words that some people do not know.
  • Protective equipment: helmets and ear protection make speaking harder.
  • Attitudes: anger, fear or lack of trust stop people listening.
  • Time pressure: rushed instructions are often misunderstood.

Overcoming barriers

  • Give important instructions away from the noise, for example at the start-of-shift meeting.
  • Use simple words and short sentences.
  • Use the language your team understands best, or a trusted interpreter.
  • Show as well as tell: demonstrate the task.
  • Use agreed hand signals on the noisy floor.
  • Ask the person to repeat the instruction back to check understanding.

lessons.title: Speaking, listening and writing at work
lessons.html:
Giving clear instructions

A good instruction says what, who, when, how and why. For example: Thabo, from now until the break, please work on the brisket station. Sterilise the saw after every carcass, because the inspector found contamination this morning.

Active listening

  • Stop what you are doing and look at the person.
  • Let them finish without interrupting.
  • Ask questions to understand.
  • Summarise what you heard: So you are saying the steriliser at station 4 is not getting hot?
  • Respond, even if only to say when you will act.

Non-verbal communication

Tone of voice, facial expression and body language send strong messages. Shouting, pointing fingers or rolling your eyes damages respect, even if your words are correct. Stay calm, especially when correcting someone.

Written communication

Supervisors write shift reports, incident reports, memos and notices.

  • Write facts, not opinions or rumours.
  • Include date, time, place and names.
  • Keep it short and clear, with one idea per sentence.
  • Check spelling and numbers before sending.
  • Notices should be short, in plain language, and placed where people will see them.

Telephone and radio

Say who you are and where you are calling from. Give the message clearly and confirm the action. On a radio, keep messages short and wait for the other person to acknowledge.

lessons.title: Working relationships across the abattoir
lessons.html:
Interoffice and interdepartmental relationships

The slaughter floor depends on other departments: procurement (buying animals), maintenance, cleaning, quality control, meat inspection, dispatch, sales, human resources and finance. Good relationships make problems easier to solve.

Building good working relationships

  • Respect: treat everyone with courtesy, whatever their position.
  • Reliability: do what you say you will do, when you said you would.
  • Information sharing: tell other departments what they need to know early, for example a breakdown that will delay dispatch.
  • Understanding their pressures: dispatch has customer deadlines; maintenance has limited staff; the inspector has legal duties.
  • Solving, not blaming: focus on fixing the problem.

The meat inspector

The inspector is not part of production and has legal authority under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Treat inspection decisions with respect, even when they slow the line. If you disagree, discuss it calmly and escalate to management or the veterinarian; never argue in front of workers or pressure the inspector.

Handling disagreements

  1. Speak to the person directly and privately.
  2. Describe the problem and its effect, not the person.
  3. Listen to their side.
  4. Look for a solution that works for both.
  5. If you cannot agree, involve your manager.

Meetings

Short daily meetings with other supervisors and departments help coordination. Prepare, stick to the agenda, agree actions with names and dates, and follow up.

Key points

  • Communication needs a sender, a channel, a receiver and feedback.
  • Noise, language and protective equipment are common barriers on the floor.
  • Give instructions that say what, who, when, how and why, and check understanding.
  • Listen actively and watch your tone and body language.
  • Respect the meat inspector's legal authority and resolve disagreements privately.
